text.title: Stakeholder Management Core Rules
text.summary: 16 testable rules grounding Stakeholder Management plus the universal skip/run routing pair (referenced by the decision tree). Stakeholder types, Power/Interest grid with mandatory attitude dimension, engagement levels, and the four-step identification-to-execution process.

section.title: Background

list.item: End Users: customers, employees — need value from product
Decision Makers: executives, sponsors — need business outcomes
Influencers: advisors, thought leaders — need credibility and early access
Builders: developers, designers — need clear requirements
Support: customer success, sales — need product knowledge
External: partners, regulators — need compliance and compatibility
High Power, High Interest → Manage Closely: engage deeply, regular bidirectional updates, co-creation where possible
High Power, Low Interest → Keep Satisfied: periodic updates, frame in terms of business outcomes, not details
Low Power, High Interest → Keep Informed: involve in feedback sessions, one-way updates are sufficient for most
Low Power, Low Interest → Monitor: minimal effort, periodic check-ins only
Partner: active collaboration, co-creation, regular meetings, bidirectional input loops
Involved: regular input, reviews, feedback sessions

section.p: The four-step process (identify, analyze, plan engagement, execute and adapt) is laid out as steps in 04-procedure.xml.

rule.statement: Every stakeholder MUST be plotted on a Power/Interest grid with an explicit attitude column (Supporter / Neutral / Resistor); grids missing the attitude column MUST be rejected.
rule.rationale: Power/Interest alone treats supporters and resistors as identical; the attitude column is the gate against blindsiding by a high-power resistor.

rule.statement: Every stakeholder row MUST have a named owner (single person) and an engagement cadence (weekly / biweekly / monthly / quarterly); orphan rows MUST be deleted or assigned.
rule.rationale: Orphan stakeholders are the source of 'nobody told me' escalations; the named-owner + cadence pair is the only durable contract.

rule.statement: Each SDD transition (backlog → todo, todo → in-progress, in-progress → done) MUST list named approvers; transitions without approvers MUST hard-fail.
rule.rationale: Implicit approval distributes accountability across nobody; explicit approval gates are the only structural defence against rework.

rule.statement: Stakeholder updates MUST be tailored to the recipient's attitude + power; broadcast updates to mixed-attitude lists are forbidden except for canonical metric rollups.
rule.rationale: Broadcast updates trigger the loudest resistor and burn supporter goodwill; tailored channels neutralise both failure modes.

rule.statement: Resistors MUST be re-engaged within 7 days of detection with a 1:1 (not email), with the 1:1 outcome logged on the register.
rule.rationale: Resistors who go silent escalate to executive sponsor blocks 80% of the time; the 7-day 1:1 is the only structural intercept.

rule.statement: Always add an explicit attitude column (Supporter / Neutral / Resistor) to the Power/Interest grid. Mark Unknown when attitude cannot be inferred from a cited source. Never leave attitude blank.
rule.rationale: A Power/Interest grid without the attitude dimension is a 2D map of a 3D problem. A high-power stakeholder coded as "Manage Closely" but secretly a Resistor is the silent killer of cross-functional product launches.

rule.statement: Every stakeholder must have a named engagement cadence (weekly 1:1, biweekly email, monthly review). "Ad-hoc" is code for "nothing happens".
rule.rationale: A communication plan without a concrete cadence produces the same outcome as no plan — stakeholders feel ignored, resistors go undetected, and late-stage blockers emerge at critical milestones.

rule.statement: The register must include these columns: name, role, interest (H/M/L), power (H/M/L), attitude (Supporter/Neutral/Resistor/Unknown), engagement level (Partner/Involved/Informed/Monitor), owner. The owner column is non-optional — "whole team manages this exec" means nobody does.
rule.rationale: Without a named owner per stakeholder relationship, escalations have no clear path and engagement drifts to whoever is most available rather than most informed.

rule.statement: Cite the source for every Power and Attitude classification (meeting notes, org chart, repo CODEOWNERS). Mark Unknown if no source exists, not a guess.
rule.rationale: LLM-generated stakeholder analyses hallucinate stakeholders from project-type templates. Requiring a source for each classification catches fabricated rows before they drive engagement decisions.

rule.statement: Define the escalation path with real names and backups: Issue → PM → (24h unresolved) → Director → (48h unresolved) → Executive sponsor. "Escalate to Director" with no name is unactionable at 11pm.
rule.rationale: Escalation paths with role names instead of person names fail when roles turn over or when multiple people hold the role. Named individuals with backup contacts are actionable; role labels are not.

rule.statement: Tie register review to the same cadence as roadmap review (quarterly minimum). Never let the PM update the register unilaterally — refresh as a 30-minute team meeting so others can flag attitude shifts the PM misses.
rule.rationale: Register rot is the most common failure: a doc built at kick-off stays unchanged while the exec sponsor leaves, attitudes shift, and new blockers emerge. Team review catches changes no single person sees.

rule.statement: Maintain a "former stakeholders" archive, not just the current list. When someone moves on, record exit and reason — never delete the row. Future PMs need the context.
rule.rationale: Stakeholder history informs future relationship-building. Knowing why a previous exec became a resistor prevents repeating the same mistake with their successor.

rule.statement: Pair the register with a decision log. Each Partner-tier stakeholder must appear in the decision log monthly or be downgraded. Engagement that does not produce decisions is theater.
rule.rationale: A stakeholder coded as "Partner" but absent from decision records is actually receiving "Inform"-level engagement. The decision log makes the gap visible before the relationship deteriorates.

rule.statement: Never let an agent autonomously change a stakeholder's engagement level from Partner to Informed. Changing someone's engagement level is a relationship downgrade with political consequences. Agent suggests, human approves.
rule.rationale: Automated downgrade of a Partner-tier stakeholder to Informed can read as a snub or signal of project de-prioritization. The consequences are relationship damage that cannot be undone with a follow-up email.

rule.statement: Run password-scrubber-agent or equivalent before committing any register or comms-plan artifact. Registers contain personal contact details, internal email addresses, sometimes phone numbers. Never let a register land in a public repo without scrubbing.
rule.rationale: PII leakage via stakeholder registers is a GDPR and internal-trust risk. Agents push to git and it becomes public without a scrubbing step.

rule.statement: For external/customer stakeholders, separate the register from any marketing CRM. Cross-link by ID, never duplicate contact data.
rule.rationale: Duplicated customer lists in the register and CRM drift out of sync. When opt-out status changes in the CRM, the unlinked register continues to drive communications to opted-out users.

rule.statement: If preconditions in `## Applies If` do not ALL hold OR any disqualifier in `## Skip If` fires, the agent MUST skip this methodology and document the skip reason in the cycle artefact.
rule.rationale: A minimum-form decision tree must route 'preconditions-not-satisfied' to skip; this rule is the canonical target.

rule.statement: If preconditions in `## Applies If` ALL hold AND no disqualifier fires, the agent MUST run the methodology end-to-end and produce the artefact specified in 02-output-contract.xml.
rule.rationale: Pair to skip-this-methodology; together they form the always-present minimal route.
